item.title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmge4exg44v5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires - Published Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country. Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday. Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993. The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa. Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution. The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation. According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes." The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said. The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president. Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities. Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200. While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country. - Published1 September - Published27 August

item.title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly7y5gvxlmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials - Published The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration. Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep in January. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest. One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said. A White House spokeswoman in a statement called the lawsuits "baseless". The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good. Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed." "We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children. In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death", according to the family's lawyer. It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees. The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border tsar Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents and private actors". "Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci told Thursday's news conference. In her statement, Lauren Bis, a spokeswoman for the White House, said the deaths of Americans at the hands of illegal immigrants should merit "equal coverage" by news media. She also said the government will "vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits". Trump had initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, wilfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake". The White House also shared a comment from Trump where he said: "I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person - but her actions were pretty tough." He also said ICE agents' work "is being made very difficult" and that "when you look at the way that car was pulled away… there are a couple versions of that tape that are very very bad," according to the comments. Good was a 37-year-old mother of three who had just moved to the city. She was shot on 7 January in a traffic stop, which immigration authorities said occurred after she made "an attempt to kill or cause bodily harm to agents". Witnesses disputed that she had been attempting to attack officers. Her death sparked nationwide protests that intensified after another Minneapolis resident, Alex Pretti, was killed by immigration agents on 24 January. Weeks later, hundreds of federal agents were withdrawn from the city and the official in charge of the operation, Greg Bovino, was removed from his post. Granger, Good's brother, said at Thursday's news conference that "since her death no meaningful change has occurred". "Our family is waiting and we will wait no longer," he said. At least 10 people have been killed in encounters with immigration officers during Trump's second term, which began in January 2025, according to the Associated Press. On Tuesday, Good's mother testified at a congressional hearing, saying: "I am a registered Republican. I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States. "But far more than being a Republican, I am a Christian," she continued. "Jesus teaches us to forgive and I have, but what we are asking for is accountability." Related topics - Published25 January - Published13 January

item.title: Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
item.description:

========================================
Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned - Published Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say. The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region. A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes. "It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic. He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT). Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion. He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters. There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage. The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment. Meanwhile, Ethiopia's foreign ministry has said it is closing its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea and expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security". Earlier, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government denied that it was backing the new rebel alliance. - Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? - Published23 hours ago - WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? - Published4 days ago Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives. Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa. There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut. Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle. In the southern Tigrayan town of Alamata, a medic told the BBC on Wednesday that 52 civilians had died in three days of heavy fighting. The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports. A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency. Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF. The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups. One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines. But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations. He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges. "The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya. Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF. But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports. Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity. As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas. The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas. Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events. item.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2z23xj555o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names - Published Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry. The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites. Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%. She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months. Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September. "The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence." Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk. Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments. She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded. One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit. For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later. Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday. He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI. SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said. Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature. Correction 1 October: An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men.com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men.com, is a legitimate business activity. item.title: Japan raises permanent residency fee by 20 times
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y8z8xeg8j1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Japan raises permanent residency fee by 20 times - Published Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955). Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements. Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours. The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population. In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations". Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage. Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change. Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year. In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows. "To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote. Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay. From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more. Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts. Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024. Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike. The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents. "My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC. "There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term." From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported. Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

Kanye West's Russia shows officially cancelled after weeks of uncertainty - Published Two stadium gigs in Russia by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, have officially been cancelled. West had been due to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October. But there was confusion in the lead-up to the shows, as the venue had said it wouldn't host him for what would have been the biggest show by a western artist since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. In a post on messaging app Telegram, gig organisers Say Agency confirmed the concerts had been cancelled with "sincere regret". "We will issue an official statement regarding the status of the project and our plans in the near future." Gazprom Arena said in August that it had not signed a rental agreement with the concert promoters and so the gig could not take place on its site. item.title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/cwgkvyyg8115o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year? - Published For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity. With just two months left of the defined hurricane season, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all. This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane. The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific. The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this. With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes. September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity. But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic. There were, however, four named tropical storms that formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna. All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic. The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least. Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El Niño is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks. As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible. In the historical Atlantic hurricane database, there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed. How does El Niño affect tropical development? While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe. As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height. Strong winds blowing at different speeds and directions at higher altitudes rip apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes. Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns. The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes. This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major. In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point. El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December. - Published11 September - Published22 September

Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents - Published Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek. Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain. The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint. On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title. "It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport. "When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality." Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China. She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter. Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent. Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury. "She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong. Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title. Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way. "To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong. "I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense." The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025. The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023. Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China. If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili. "MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong. The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira. When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response. "I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said. item.title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3y0zx822wlzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why - Published Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car. Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys. It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car. Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern. So what could explain these reports of motion sickness? Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles. It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says. "I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles. But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive. Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point". "There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says. 'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell' When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it. She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell. On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before. Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars. Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says. But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds. What could cause it? Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness. Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles. Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says. Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration. "It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac. This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time". Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness. Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly. She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself. Some features of electric cars may feel unfamiliar to drivers at first, adds Mike Hawes, head of the Society of Motor Manufacturers. He says EVs can offer a different driving experience. "However, drivers typically adjust quickly to these characteristics, and many models also allow regenerative braking to be tailored to individual preferences." Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, according to Hac, and experts say women and children are more susceptible. Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF. Hold your head still and open the window As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , external At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030. Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy. The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific". Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness. - Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a book - Sit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front window - Keep your head still by holding it against the headrest - Recline your seat - Regulate your breathing - Open the window to let in fresh air - Take travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsiness - Before a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy food Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says. There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration. Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly". But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough. Get in touch Are you an EV driver or have been a passenger in an EV? Have you experienced nausea due to motion sickness? Tell us your story.

item.title: The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
item.description:

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part' - Published "I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk." "I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her." Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa. The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township. "Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am." At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust. At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve. He raises his fist. "We are men!" he shouts. The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer. "Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide." Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women. The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women. The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women. South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer. The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder. A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners. For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions. "We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here." Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation. Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done. The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late. "When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?" He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again." Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains. "And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity. "We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence." He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men. "You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe." Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges. Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women. Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court. But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever. Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket. "We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says. "We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?" It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko. She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve. "Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?" Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other." Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer. Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up. "As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this. "And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends." Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard. "I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better." item.title: The vanishing world of India's street magicians
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck7v4v8pmzdeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The vanishing world of India's street magicians - Published Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air. The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame. These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick. "The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator." Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft. Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession. Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces. There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana. Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries. Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers. "For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains. Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous. The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it. He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka. His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan. Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded. As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations. One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan. Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day. Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces. Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink. "Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance." Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline. "With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says. It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces. For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed. Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur. Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land. "This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra. For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse. When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back. "We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities." For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased. Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia. Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard. Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees. "Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says. The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts. "There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says. For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it. "A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says. His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind. Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm. "I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said. Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out. "I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says. item.title: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d949gq47x9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's - Published Reporter Michael Graczyk has covered nearly 500 executions carried out in Texas, continuing even after his 2018 retirement from The Associated Press. He remembers two instances where needles popped out before reinsertion for successful execution - but never one in which an inmate survived. That's what happened this week in Tennessee, when 50-year-old inmate Christa Pike remained breathing and audibly snoring after two separate doses of pentobarbital, the barbiturate used in the state's lethal injection protocol. Graczyk, 76, says he wasn't entirely surprised to hear of the anomaly - and had actually thought about the possibility during his decades-long career as a Texas journalist. "It seems to me it was just a matter of time," he told BBC News. Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set. Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative. Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer. It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, describes a botched execution as one with "unanticipated problems or delays that caused, at least arguably, unnecessary agony for the prisoner or that reflect gross incompetence of the executioner". The organisation has compiled a list of 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set. But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered. "That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State. Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job. "There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said. There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre, which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people. "I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said. "That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened." Although he is technically retired, he still works freelance for AP covering executions in his home state. He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news. "I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been." "Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right." Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess". Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said. "So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up." In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites. During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said. He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley. Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words. "He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore." That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years. "To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection." When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious. "Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said. But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done". Related topics - Published12 hours ago - Published21 October 2023

item.title: School protests send shivers down French government's spine
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69wzjjxex8po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
School protests send shivers down French government's spine - Published It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble. Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth. Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in. Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away. For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed. Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats". A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country. On Thursday – the high point so far – hundreds of lycées (where 15-18 year-olds finish their schooling) were being blockaded. On Friday, the situation had improved but around 400 lycées were closed in order to protect staff and students. Universities are beginning to join in. Violence has erupted. On Thursday the main hall of a lycée in Nantes was destroyed by fire. Smaller fires too numerable to mention were lit at school entrance gates around the country. The cost of the damage is millions of euros. According to Education Minister Édouard Geffray, 65 teaching staff including 40 school heads have been injured. "Most of the staff who were hurt said that the people they were facing… were not their own pupils," he said. In addition, the government says that around 300 police and firefighters have been treated for injuries, and some 2,000 people – mainly minors – taken into custody. For their part, student groups say they have a long list of people injured by police. Two teenagers have serious eye injuries and one has lost many of his teeth. The problem would be hard enough if it was just a question of meeting the protesters' demands. But there is another dimension – a political and social one – which makes this student crisis far more dangerous than in the past. The demands do exist, even if they remain vague. They are about money – the lack of it – and the need for more teachers, smaller classes and better buildings. On such matters, many in France would agree with the teenagers. Certainly using protest to demand money from government is such a national habit that even governments agree it's legitimate. And of course, things are indeed getting worse in the education system – because money is so tight. This week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu published his draft for next year's budget. The motif is "More cuts – and this time we're serious!" Whether or not he manages to remove €54bn (£46bn) from state spending, as he promises, remains open to question. But it is surely obvious that the era of public largesse to defuse social unrest in France is now in its twilight. Students demanding an extra school nurse or insulation in the dining-block are likely to be disappointed. But that is the lesser of the worries. The far greater fear is that these student protests are being manipulated by the hard left – and that the violence of recent days is a foretaste of what awaits a dangerously polarised society in the year of elections that is coming. For the right and centre, there is no doubt that behind the student trouble lies the cunning hand of the France Unbowed party (LFI) and its popular presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. LFI leaders have regularly appeared next to the students – notably in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis whose mayor Bally Bagayoko was criticised for saying that "violence can sometimes be legitimate." An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI." It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections". In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook. The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests". But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing. Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated. But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count. Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen. If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

item.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vgyg824m02o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times. Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers. Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit". Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago. Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too. Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states. So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato? Spain accused of self-interest Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day. Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault. That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests. "It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations. "I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves." Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries. "Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone." Rising Chinese investment According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants. Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe". "US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me. The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry. Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally. According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably. China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran. That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US. And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro. "Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo. But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market. There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles. However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical. "France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says. But there's also the question of security. On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds. This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year. MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole. "When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February. Juan Ignacio Zoido Álvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk". Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion. "As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me. "Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe." More emerging alliances Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances. Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity. In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato. Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country. No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles. Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank. "There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA). "Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me. In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality". Greece's shift Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me. In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere. In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles. There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected". He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else. With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times. But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis. He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want. That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers. Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles. However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities. Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.
